speaker_role: student/content creator sharing personal experience (self-described, not an admissions professional)
commercial_incentive: none evident in transcript beyond building his own YouTube channel/personal brand
key_insights: Says competitive applications typically need at least three recommendation letters: one counselor plus two teachers.
Recommends STEM-track students get one STEM teacher and one non-STEM teacher (and the reverse for non-STEM-track students) to show range.
Argues a bad or generic-sounding rec letter is a near-universal red flag even at schools that don't weigh recommendations heavily.
Says junior-year teachers are usually the best choices since they taught you most recently and can be asked easily at the start of senior year.
Recommends entering each school year with 2-3 teachers in mind as potential recommenders, based on early rapport, and cultivating those relationships all year.
Suggests deliberately over-investing effort on ungraded assignments, since most classmates ignore them, as a way to get a teacher's attention.
Claims that visibly attentive classroom behavior (note-taking, non-disruptive questions, volunteering, engaging one-on-one after class) builds the personal rapport that produces stronger letters.

Argues that building outside-class relationships (club advisors, multi-year teachers) and public recognition for extracurricular projects (e.g., local news coverage) further deepens a teacher's willingness to write a standout letter.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker claims (unsupported) that going above and beyond on an assignment gets noticed by a teacher about 70% of the time.
Speaker says following his baseline steps yields roughly a 'six to seven out of ten' rec letter.
notable_or_distinctive: Unusually granular, personal step-by-step social strategy for building teacher rapport over multiple years, going beyond generic 'be a good student' advice into specific classroom behaviors.
reliability_notes: Long video (4,571 words) built on the creator's own unverified personal anecdotes and self-reported success; percentages and rankings (e.g., '70% chance,' 'six to seven out of ten letter') are made up estimates, not data, and the advice reflects one individual's social approach rather than confirmed admissions-office practice.
